title: Spring Boot 3 AOT Engine & GraalVM Native Image Reflection Hints
prerequisites: Understanding of JIT vs AOT compilation and reflection

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A chef normally cooks each dish when it's ordered (JIT — the JVM compiles code at runtime). A frozen-meal factory instead prepares everything in advance and freezes it (AOT — compile ahead of time): the meal is ready in seconds when needed. But the frozen meal is rigid: if a customer wants a dish with 'whatever ingredients are in the fridge' (reflection — deciding at runtime), the frozen meal can't adapt because everything was decided when it was made. So the factory must know in advance every possible ingredient combo and write it on the box — that's the reflection-hints step.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Spring Boot's AOT engine processes your app at build time and generates the metadata GraalVM Native Image needs: it pre-computes bean definitions, condition evaluations, and registers reflection/classpath hints. The result: a native executable with fast startup and low memory. Build with the Maven plugin: mvn -Pnative native:compile (needs GraalVM + native-image). Startup drops from seconds to milliseconds. Caveats: reflection, proxies, and dynamic features must be known at build time — sometimes you add hints via @RegisterReflectionHint, RuntimeHintsRegistrar, or imports.yaml.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Spring Boot 3's AOT engine runs a build-time pass that creates a 'pre-initialized' application context model: it evaluates @Conditional logic, resolves bean definitions, and generates code/classes that GraalVM can compile natively. Native Image performs a static analysis (points-to analysis) of reachable code and requires ALL reflective accesses, dynamic proxies, and resource loads to be registered up front — anything discovered at runtime by reflection is 'unknown' and gets pruned or fails. Spring's AOT generates RuntimeHints (reflection, resource, serialization, proxy hints) from the analyzed bean graph, and you can contribute your own via RuntimeHintsRegistrar.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The build process: Spring Boot AOT invokes an AOT engine that runs the ApplicationContext 'in a headless way', collects BeanDefinitions, evaluates conditions, and emits (1) generated source/classes (e.g. the initialized context), and (2) RuntimeHints (registered classes for reflection, resources, JDK proxies, serialization). GraalVM's native-image then performs a static points-to analysis from the main entry point, builds the native executable with the registered hints, and uses a closed-world assumption — no dynamic class loading, no runtime reflection unless hinted. The result has no JIT and no class files; it runs with a Substrate VM. Missing hints manifest as ReflectionNotRegisteredException (java.lang.NoSuchMethodException via reflection) at runtime.

codeComparison.title: JVM deployment vs GraalVM native image
codeComparison.summary: A JVM jar starts in seconds and supports runtime reflection; a native image starts in milliseconds but requires all dynamic features to be declared at build time.

legacyOrBad.label: JVM jar deployment
legacyOrBad.snippet: java -jar app.jar  # ❌ OLD: JIT — fast to build, slow to start, high memory

fullFile.code:
#!/bin/bash
# ❌ OLD: Classic JVM deployment. The JIT compiles hot code at runtime,
# so startup takes seconds (class loading + JIT warmup) and the JVM
# reserves significant memory (heap, metaspace, JIT code cache). For
# serverless/lambda-style workloads this cold start is expensive and
# the memory footprint costs money.
java -jar app.jar

# Advantages: full reflection/proxies work at runtime, no build-time
# analysis needed, quick builds, familiar tooling.

modernOrGood.label: GraalVM native image
modernOrGood.snippet:
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile   # ✅ NEW: AOT + native image build
./target/app   # ✅ NEW: native executable — starts in milliseconds

fullFile.code:
#!/bin/bash
# ✅ NEW: Spring Boot 3 AOT + GraalVM Native Image. The AOT engine
# generates hints at build time; native-image compiles a native
# executable that starts in milliseconds and uses far less memory.

# Build (requires GraalVM with native-image):
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile

# Run:
./target/demo-app

# If a reflective lookup fails at runtime (e.g. a library uses
# reflection on your classes), register it:
# import org.springframework.aot.hint.annotation.RegisterReflectionHint;
# @RegisterReflectionHint(classes = SomeModel.class)

# Or via a RuntimeHintsRegistrar bean for fine-grained control.

interviewGotchas.question: Why does reflection break in native images, and how does Spring Boot's AOT engine solve it?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This is the defining native-image concept — interviewers want the closed-world assumption and the hint-generation mechanism, because naive ports of JVM apps fail exactly here.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: GraalVM Native Image builds with a closed-world assumption: it statically analyzes reachable code and compiles it into the executable; there is no JVM class loader that can find classes at runtime, and reflective lookups (Class.forName, getDeclaredMethod, dynamic proxies) only work for entities explicitly registered at build time. Reflection that isn't hinted fails at runtime with NoSuchMethodError/ClassNotFoundException-style errors. Spring Boot 3's AOT engine mitigates this by running the application context model at build time: it discovers beans, evaluates conditions, and generates RuntimeHints (reflection, resources, serialization, JDK proxies) for everything Spring needs, so the native build includes them. Custom reflection (e.g. a library that reflects over YOUR model classes) must be registered manually — the AOT engine cannot know about arbitrary reflective access.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'native image just compiles the jar to a binary'. The closed-world model changes what is possible: no dynamic class loading, no unregistered reflection. Another trap: assuming Spring Boot AOT covers all reflection automatically — it covers Spring's own usage; third-party/reflective libraries need explicit hints. Candidates who describe the closed-world assumption and hint registration show real native-image experience.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the trade-off between a native image and a JVM deployment beyond startup speed?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the honest engineering trade-off — interviewers want peak throughput and flexibility considerations, not just 'native is faster'.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Native images win on startup (ms vs seconds) and memory footprint (significantly lower RSS), which matters for serverless, autoscaling, and containerized fleets. They lose on peak throughput: without a JIT, there is no runtime adaptive optimization, so long-running CPU-heavy workloads are often slower than a warmed-up JVM (C2-optimized code). Other costs: build time (minutes, needs GraalVM and enough memory), build-time analysis constraints (all dynamic behavior must be declared), and a smaller ecosystem of compatible libraries. The right choice: native for cold-start-sensitive, short-lived, I/O-bound services; JVM for long-lived CPU-intensive services where JIT pays off. Spring also supports both — the AOT hints are only used for native, while the JVM path is unchanged.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'native images are faster everywhere'. JIT warm-up can beat AOT for long-running CPU-bound workloads. Another trap: thinking you can mix — a native image is all-or-nothing for the closed-world; you cannot lazily load a JVM plugin at runtime. Candidates who weigh cold start vs steady-state throughput show real engineering judgment.
